transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because... I keep hearing Garrett’s voice. It’s so clear, it’s exactly like he’s standing right behind me when I'm out on the trail. We used to hike a lot, actually, mostly up near the ridge where the cedar trees get really thick. The smell of cedar is just fantastic up there, especially after it rains. But lately I’ve been spending more time in my painting room, and I hear him in there, too. I’ve been working with oils mostly—linseed oil has this very distinct smell, it gets into your clothes, your hair, it's almost impossible to wash out... 

Anyway, the thing is, the rational part of me, the part that studied psychology, knows he’s dead. I know that. But when I hear him speak, in that exact moment... it just feels completely real. Like I could just turn around and ask him to hand me a brush. I prefer the flat bristle brushes for landscapes, they give you much better texture on the canvas when you're trying to capture the light through the trees... but yes, the voice. That's why I'm here.
Do you experience any other sensations or perceptions that others don't, like seeing, feeling, or smelling things that aren't there?

No, no, it's really just the hearing him part. I don't see him standing there, and I definitely don't smell or feel anything that isn't actually in the room. Well, I mean, I do have a very sharp sense of smell in general. Always have. Even back when I was doing my undergrad, I could tell if someone opened a pack of peppermint gum three rows back in the lecture hall. It was a massive hall, too, the kind with those terrible fold-out wooden desks that completely wreck your posture. Ergonomics are so incredibly important, especially now that everyone is glued to their phones and laptops all day. I actually read a fascinating paper recently about how cervical spine misalignment might subtly affect mood regulation and cognitive fatigue over time... but, um. What was I saying? Right, no. To answer your question, no phantom smells or seeing things. Just his voice.
Do you hear Garrett’s voice even when you’re not thinking about him or feeling sad about his death?

Well, that’s the interesting thing about it. It’s not really about feeling sad. I mean, obviously I went through the normal grieving process when he passed, but the voice... it wasn't a part of that ordinary grief. I only started hearing him recently, during this really wired stretch I had. I was barely sleeping at all, maybe an hour or two a night, but I just felt this intense, unrelenting drive to keep going. 

I started taking on these completely impossible projects. Like, I decided to completely strip and refinish all the antique cabinets in my kitchen in a single weekend. Have you ever worked with chemical wood strippers? You have to be so incredibly careful, the fumes are just noxious, and you need this very specific fine grade of steel wool to get the old varnish out of the wood grain. I actually went and bought out the entire stock of grade 0000 steel wool at the local hardware store at six in the morning. The guy at the counter, Jim, he’s always there, he was wearing this incredibly bright orange vest that honestly violates basic color theory, just terrible for the eyes... but anyway, I was buying that and gallons of mineral spirits. Mineral spirits actually double as a great cleaner for my oil brushes, so that worked out perfectly for my painting room. 

But um... right, what were we saying? The voice. Yeah, I had never heard him like that before that massive mood shift. It was only when I was in that wired state, just buzzing and taking on the world, that he started talking to me. It definitely wasn't just ordinary grief. Ordinary grief is heavy, you know? It makes you want to sleep. But I wasn't sleeping at all.

Have you ever had periods where your mood was extremely elevated, you felt like you had more energy than usual, or you were doing things more rapidly or impulsively, like when you were working intensely on projects?

Yes, exactly. At first, I felt almost... lit up, you know? Like I had this incredible, urgent purpose that no one else could see. I was just buzzing with it. 

Actually, speaking of being lit up, I ended up changing out every single lightbulb in my house during that stretch because the color temperature was completely wrong. People really underestimate how much ambient lighting impacts circadian rhythms and cortisol levels. I mean, as a psychologist, I’ve read so many papers on how blue light exposure disrupts melatonin synthesis, which is why I absolutely refuse to use fluorescent tubes. Plus, they have that terrible 60-hertz hum. It just drills right into your skull. My grandmother had this ancient refrigerator that made the exact same humming noise, it used to rattle the floorboards in her kitchen. She kept all these little ceramic roosters on top of it, and they would just clink together all night... 

Wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, the energy. Yeah, so I had all this urgent purpose, but the thing was, if anyone questioned what I was doing or tried to slow me down even a little bit, I would just snap into absolute rage. Just furious.

Have you ever had a period lasting at least a week where your mood was consistently extremely elevated, expansive, or irritable, along with a noticeable increase in your energy or activity levels, not just brief moments here and there?

Well, yes, it was definitely for more than a week. It felt like it went on for a long time. I was just going and going. I was staying up all night writing these complete, detailed outlines for entirely new treatment programs. I mean, I was emailing colleagues at two in the morning, offering to mentor extra people, just taking on all this stuff. And at the same time, I was starting all these new canvases in my painting room. Just all at once, even though none of it was actually realistic for one person to do. 

But, you know, the canvases I use are these beautiful heavy-duty linen ones. I have to order them from this specific supplier in New York because the local stores just sell that cheap cotton duck stuff that warps if you look at it wrong. Cotton is so absorbent, it just drinks the oil right out of the paint, and then your colors get all dull and sunken in. The old masters, like Rembrandt and Vermeer, they knew how to prepare a surface. They used rabbit skin glue to size the canvas. I actually tried making my own rabbit skin glue once, but the smell when you heat it up in the double boiler is just... it's atrocious. It smells exactly like wet dog mixed with old shoes. I had to open all the windows in the house, which was a disaster because it was November and freezing, and then my heating bill was astronomical that month... 

Um, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the energy. Yeah, it was definitely a solid week or more of just doing all of that at once, completely non-stop.
During that period of high energy and activity, did you also experience a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, or trouble focusing on tasks?

Yeah, the sleep thing, like I said, I was barely sleeping at all, maybe an hour or two. But the thoughts... man, my thoughts were just flying. It's like they were racing so fast I couldn't even grab onto them. I'd start out with one simple idea, like, oh, I need to finish this one patient note, right? And before I knew it, that one thought would explode into five massive new projects, and then suddenly I'm thinking about this hike I took in the Adirondacks three years ago. The trails up there are incredible in the fall, the sugar maples turn this unbelievable shade of crimson. You have to make sure you have the right boots, though, because the shale gets really slick after a rain. I actually bought these Italian leather hiking boots that were supposed to be waterproof, but they totally leaked on the first trip, which was so frustrating because they cost a fortune. I tried treating them with mink oil, but... 

Wait, sorry. The thoughts. Yeah, so it would go from the patient note, to the five projects, to the hike, and then completely out of nowhere, I'd just be slammed with all this intense guilt about Garrett's funeral. All of that in the span of a few seconds, before I could even catch my breath or figure out what I was originally doing. So yeah, trouble focusing is an understatement.
